Contribution: Compliance accommodates geometric and positional uncertainty [1]; reviews note the limits of vision alone [2]; grasp synthesis has largely targeted rigid objects with learned or analytic quality metrics [17,18].
Gap relative to this study: Compliance does not say where on a thin ring to make contact; the contact stage here combines compliant pads with a six-axis wrist force sensor.

Contribution: Perception, physical-property estimation, planning and feedback are treated as coupled components; model-based planning for deformable linear objects [3]; review of pushing and grasping [5].
Gap relative to this study: Addresses cables and elastomers rather than a stiff spring-steel ring; motivates the discrete pre-contact and continuous post-contact split used here.

Contribution: Task board with an elastic-deformation (circlip) module [6]; benchmarking of off-the-shelf solutions on NIST task boards, with limited scene awareness and error recovery [7]; retaining-ring machine with fixed tooling [8]; impedance-based interaction control [19].
Gap relative to this study: No auditable grasp-selection layer that couples circlip geometry, expansion strain, force demand and seating-induced tilt.

Contribution: Reviews of quantum computation for dynamic optimization [9,20]; Grover search, amplitude amplification and optimal iteration counts [21–23]; classical matching of claimed quantum advantages [24]; open-source tools (Quirk, fake backends, Rust libraries) [10–16]; quantum-inspired multi-objective optimizers for feature selection, scheduling, logistics and energy systems [27]–[37].
Gap relative to this study: Used here only as an algorithmic template on a 16-candidate problem, with noise testing and no claim of advantage (Sections 3.6 and 6.2).

Contribution: Elastic split-ring (circlip) assembly with seating tilt as primary endpoint; a deliberately small, inspectable quantum-inspired candidate space; a protocol that separates circuit-level robustness from robot-level evidence.
Gap relative to this study: Novelty is to be substantiated by a systematic literature search (Section 7).
